design_detail: Follow-up interview study of two random samples of US Army enlisted men and draftees who left Vietnam for the United States in September 1971: a 'general sample' of 470 drawn from about 13,760 returnees, and a 'drug-positive sample' of 495 drawn from about 1,400 whose urine at departure was positive for narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates (22 men were in both; 943 selected). One structured interview 8 to 12 months after return (May to September 1972) asked about drug use before service, in Vietnam and since return; a urine specimen was taken at interview and military and Veterans Administration records were sought. Prevalence results are for the general sample (451 interviewed); predictor analyses combine both samples with the drug-positive sample weighted (automatic interaction detector and multiple classification analysis). The paper presents highlights; full methods and data are in a 1974 government monograph (ref. 1), not read.
can_establish: For US Army enlisted men leaving Vietnam in September 1971, the self-reported proportions who used narcotics and who met the study's own addiction criteria before service, in Vietnam and in the 8 to 12 months after return, and how few of the men addicted in Vietnam were addicted again in that first year home.
cannot_establish: Why remission was so common (the authors leave open whether the men's backgrounds or the change of social setting explains it, p. 960), whether it lasted beyond the first year, whether it happened without treatment (treatment before or after return is not reported), how it compares with remission in civilians addicted at home (the only comparison is another study's treated patients), whether it applies to women or to other places and times, or whether drug use caused the problems that went with it after return (no comparison group; one interview).

sample.recruitment: Random samples from military records: names of all Army enlisted men and draftees returning from Vietnam in September 1971 were supplied by the Department of Defense (general sample), and names of those with a positive departure urine test by the Surgeon General (drug-positive sample) (p. 956, Methods, 2nd paragraph). September 1971 was chosen as the first month with complete urine-test records and because those men's tours were thought to coincide with peak heroin use by US soldiers (p. 956, Methods, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Army enlisted men and draftees returning from Vietnam to the United States in September 1971. Drug-positive sample: departure urine positive for illicit drugs (narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates) according to the Methods (p. 956); the abstract says positive for opiates (p. 955). No exclusions stated.
sample.demographics: General sample at arrival in Vietnam (tabulation, pp. 956–957; text p. 957): all men; draftees 46%, regular army 54%; age 24 or over 15%, 22–23 17%, 21 18%, 20 34%, 19 or under 16% (half under 21); white 80%, Black 13%, Spanish-American 5%, Oriental 1%, other 1%; 67% had at least a high-school diploma; single 68%, married 29%; 90% had held a full-time civilian job. Before service, 47% had tried an illicit drug (41% a cannabis derivative, and for 17% cannabis was the only one), 11% a narcotic (largely oral codeine or codeine cough syrup) and 2% heroin; one third had been drunk weekly in the year before induction and 4% had a history of 'problems' with alcohol.
sample.attrition: Single interview, no further waves in this paper. Of the 943 selected, 95% were interviewed (898), 92% gave a urine specimen and military records were obtained for 99% (p. 956, Methods, 3rd paragraph); 451 of the 470 in the general sample were interviewed (Table 1 footnote, p. 959; 96%, editors' calculation). The men not interviewed are not described.
sample.selection_effects: One month's returnees from one service at one point in the war: young enlisted men only, no women and no officers; men who did not return home that month are outside the frame by design. The drug-positive sample was selected on a positive urine test and enters the weighted predictor analyses and, unweighted, Table 2 and the Figure. The authors state, without data, that the general sample's drug experience before service did not differ from a national sample of comparable age (p. 957, citing ref. 3).

exposure.measurement: Self-report at one interview 8 to 12 months after return, covering use before service, in Vietnam and since return; interviewers did not know which men had used drugs or which sample they came from (p. 956). Checks: 97% of men whose military records showed heroin use in Vietnam reported it at interview; urine was taken at interview, but men's expectations matched their results poorly (16% of men with a positive specimen had expected it; 42% of those expecting a positive had one), which the authors attribute partly to question design (p. 956, Methods, 3rd paragraph). The share of interview specimens positive for opiates is not reported (the Comment calls it low, p. 961). Addiction was recorded by self-report and by the study's own criteria: three of four of more-than-weekly use for more than a month; at least two of chills, stomach cramps, insomnia and muscle pain on withdrawal; withdrawal lasting at least two days, or at least 12 hours if modified; believing oneself addicted (p. 957).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Among the 196 general-sample men who tried narcotics in Vietnam: fewer than 5 times 24%; 5 or more times but not more than weekly 9%; more than weekly for under 6 months 20%, for 6–8 months 23%, for 9 months or more 25% (p. 957, tabulation). Narcotics in Vietnam were mostly smoked; injection rose with prolonged use, and 40% of men using for nine months or more had injected (pp. 957–958). After return, injection was the preferred method of 63% of men using frequently, and heroin replaced codeine as the narcotic most used (p. 959). Amounts were not recorded.
exposure.polysubstance: Alongside narcotics in Vietnam: alcohol 92%, marijuana 69% (an estimate), amphetamines 25%, barbiturates 23%; use of all three of narcotics, amphetamines and barbiturates (18% of the general sample) was the rule among men using any of them (pp. 957–958). Other drug use was handled descriptively and by grouping men by the drug class used after return (Table 3, p. 960); one comparison of post-return problems held other drug use since return constant, with no data shown (p. 960).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable in the usual sense. Remission meant not being addicted again between return and interview, a window of 8 to 12 months (on average about ten months, p. 958); many men counted as remitted used narcotics after return (Table 2, p. 959: 33% to 50% of the previously addicted groups).

comparison.controls: No comparison group of the study's own for the remission estimates. The Figure and text set men first addicted in Vietnam beside a published series of 122 patients committed for treatment under the Narcotic Addict Rehabilitation Act (NARA), six months after release to aftercare (ref. 5), described in the text as young (under 30) patients treated at the Lexington and Fort Worth federal hospitals (Figure, p. 956; p. 958). Post-return problems are compared only among veterans grouped by drug use; with no nonveteran or non-Vietnam comparison, the authors say they cannot tell whether these problems were more frequent than expected (p. 959).
comparison.matching: None. The NARA series differs in setting (civilians committed for hospital treatment), in duration of addiction (the authors note that civilians usually reach treatment after several years, p. 961) and in follow-up interval (six months after release, against eight to ten months after return).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Pre-service drug use, drinking, delinquency and family history were recalled at the same interview, one to several years later; only service status, age and education came from military records (p. 956). No pre-service psychiatric assessment.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable for the study (no external control group); not reported for the NARA series.

outcomes.instruments: Structured interview (not named; full presentation in the 1974 monograph, ref. 1), urine at interview, military records and Veterans Administration claims files (p. 956). Post-return outcomes: narcotic use graded as none, light, heavy or addiction (light and heavy are not defined in this paper); addiction by self-report and by the study's criteria; and, in Table 3, perceived drug-related problem, non-traffic arrest, psychiatric treatment, depressive syndrome, unemployment (men out of service six months or more), divorce (men ever married) and alcoholism (p. 960).
outcomes.validity_norms: Study-specific addiction criteria, not a standard diagnostic instrument; self-report checked against military records and urine (p. 956). Definitions of depressive syndrome and alcoholism are not given in this paper.
outcomes.operationalization: Remission: not addicted again between return and interview. Addiction: three of the four study criteria, or the man's own report (p. 957). 'Remission' therefore includes men who still used narcotics, lightly or heavily.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None reported. Seven post-return problems were compared across four drug-use groups in Table 3, with significance shown by symbols only and no test named; multivariate predictor analyses for narcotic use in Vietnam, narcotic use after return, heavy use after return and four post-return problems are described in words without statistics (pp. 958–960).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Interviewers did not know beforehand which men had used drugs or which sample they belonged to (p. 956).

analysis.effect_sizes: Percentages only, without confidence intervals or test statistics. Editors' calculation (Wilson 95% intervals; general sample n=451, Table 1): narcotic use in Vietnam 43% (about 38.5% to 47.6%); self-reported addiction in Vietnam 20% (16.6% to 23.9%); narcotic use since return 10% (7.6% to 13.1%); addiction since return by the study's criteria 1% (0.4% to 2.4%), about 4 to 5 men, and by self-report 0.7%, about 3 men. In the combined Table 2 group still addicted at departure (n=134), readdiction 14% (9.1% to 20.9%). The statement that only 7% of men using narcotics after return became addicted rests on about 3 of about 45 men in the general sample (editors' calculation from Table 1: 0.7% and 10% of 451).
analysis.covariates: Predictor analyses used automatic interaction detector (AID) and multiple classification analysis (MCA) on the combined samples, with the drug-positive sample weighted to its share of the general sample (p. 958); one comparison held other drug use since return constant (p. 960). Results are given in words, without coefficients, except that pre-service variables together explained 10% of the variance in pre-service drug use (p. 960).
analysis.selective_reporting: The paper presents 'highlights' and refers to the 1974 monograph for the full data (p. 955). Several analyses are described without data: the AID and MCA results; the comparison of men who had and had not used narcotics in Vietnam among those not using narcotics after return (p. 960); and the urine results at interview, the main objective check on post-return use.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Key subgroups are small: 90 general-sample men first addicted in Vietnam (Figure), Table 3 groups of 33 to 71 men, and post-return addiction in the general sample amounting to a handful of men.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In a random sample of 451 enlisted men interviewed 8 to 12 months after leaving Vietnam, 43% reported narcotic use and 20% reported addiction in Vietnam (21% met the study's criteria), against 11% narcotic use and 0.2% to 0.4% addiction before service; since return, 10% had used narcotics and 0.7% to 1% had been addicted (Table 1, p. 959). Of the men first addicted in Vietnam, a few percent were addicted again in that window (Figure: about 2% of the general sample's 90 and about 7% of the drug-positive sample's 341), while a third or more used narcotics again; among the 134 men still addicted at departure, 50% used narcotics after return and 14% were addicted again (Table 2). Heavy use of each drug class, injection and a preference for heroin over codeine were more common after return than before service (p. 959).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says usage and addiction essentially fell back to pre-Vietnam levels (p. 955), leaving out the rise in heavy use, injection and heroin preference that the results report (p. 959). The text calls the 95% remission rate one unheard of among treated US patients (p. 958), but the 95% is not tied to a stated sample or denominator, and the comparison is a different study of patients committed for treatment. The Comment concludes that, at least in certain circumstances, opiates are not so addictive that use necessarily leads to addiction or addiction to permanence (p. 961), and states the limits plainly: an atypical setting, a sample homogeneous in age, sex, occupation and period, a short tour, possible concealment and unknown generalizability (p. 961). For post-return problems the wording turns causal: the factors behind discontinuation "should probably be credited with preventing gross maladjustment" (p. 960), although the authors had just said they could not assume that drug use caused these problems (p. 959).

timeline.event: Robins, 'The Vietnam Drug User Returns' (Special Action Office monograph): the full methods and data of this study (ref. 1; on the General list as R3; not read for this card).
This paper: highlights of the first follow-up, 8 to 12 months after return.
A second follow-up about three years after return, with a matched nonveteran comparison group, is described as under way (p. 961).
Helzer, Robins & Davis, antecedents of narcotic use and addiction in the 898 veterans (Drug and Alcohol Dependence; _Dependence-epidemiology list #14; not read for this card).
Robins, on whether the veterans' rapid recovery from heroin addiction was a fluke or a normal expectation (Addiction; _Dependence-epidemiology list #11; not read for this card).
Price et al., 25-year follow-up of remission in the Vietnam cohort, with patterns of treatment use (American Journal of Public Health; General list #20; not read for this card).
Robins, the veterans three years after Vietnam and how the study changed the authors' view of heroin (American Journal on Addictions; _Dependence-epidemiology list #13; not read for this card).
Hall & Weier, methodological appraisal of Lee Robins' Vietnam studies (Addiction; _Dependence-epidemiology list #15; not read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: The circumstances (a relatively short tour of duty with inexpensive, relatively pure narcotics, then return home, p. 961) cannot be repeated, so the finding has later follow-ups of the same cohort and appraisals rather than independent replications; these are on the project's lists and were not read for this card. Within this paper, the findings concern young enlisted men within about a year of return; they cannot by themselves support statements about remission in people who come to treatment, about long-term remission, or about remission without treatment.

funding.funder: No funding statement or acknowledgement is printed. The introduction states that the White House Special Action Office for Drug Abuse Prevention (SAODAP) arranged for and assisted in the follow-up study (p. 955); the full report is a SAODAP monograph (ref. 1).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry, Washington University School of Medicine, St Louis (p. 955). Completed interviews were sent to the Addiction Research Foundation in Canada under a link-file system so that no one could connect answers to names (p. 956). The study was set up by a White House drug-policy office to plan treatment for returning soldiers; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort of people identified when regular opioid use begins rather than when they reach treatment, followed for several years with a standard diagnostic interview, repeated biological testing and a record of any treatment, beside a matched comparison group and including people who leave the setting where their use began, would show how often, for how long and under what conditions opioid addiction remits without treatment.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: The frame is the population the paper describes: all Army enlisted men and draftees returning from Vietnam in September 1971, from Department of Defense and Surgeon General lists (p. 956). How far this population stands for other people who use heroin is a question of indirectness, not of this item.

Random samples from complete lists; prevalence estimates come from the general sample, and the drug-positive sample is weighted in the predictor analyses (pp. 956, 958). Table 2 mixes the samples unweighted (see reporting issues).

451 interviews give headline prevalences to within about 4 to 5 percentage points (editors' calculation), but post-return addiction in the general sample rests on a handful of men, and remission estimates on 90 general-sample men first addicted in Vietnam.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Service status, age, race, education, marital status, work history and pre-service drug and alcohol use are tabulated for the general sample, and the setting is described (pp. 955–957).

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: 95% of the 943 men and 451 of the 470 in the general sample were interviewed (p. 956; Table 1 footnote, p. 959).

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Addiction was defined by the study's own criteria, one of which is the man's belief that he was addicted, or by self-report alone; use before and in Vietnam was recalled one to several years later; light and heavy use are not defined in this paper. Self-report agreed well with military records of heroin use (97%), but the urine results at interview, the only biological check on post-return use, are not reported (pp. 956–957, 961).

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same interview for all men, by interviewers who did not know their drug history or sample (p. 956).

Simple percentages from a random sample suit the descriptive aims, but no confidence intervals are given, significance is shown by symbols without tests, multivariate results have no coefficients, the 95% remission figure has no stated denominator, and Table 2 pools the two samples without weighting or saying so (pp. 958–960).

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Interview completion 95% overall and about 96% in the general sample (p. 956; editors' calculation).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A random sample of a defined population, interviewed almost completely by interviewers blind to drug history, with record checks: strong features for 1975. The limits on its numbers come from self-reported, partly retrospective drug use judged by non-standard criteria, an unreported urine check after return, a short window of 8 to 12 months, and thin statistical reporting. The source may be cited for the proportions who used narcotics and met the study's addiction criteria before, in and after Vietnam in this population, and for the observation that few men addicted in Vietnam were addicted again in the first year home, many of them still using narcotics. It may not be cited for remission rates in general, for remission lasting beyond a year, for remission without treatment (treatment is not reported), or for effects of drug use on post-return problems, which rest on unadjusted, cross-sectional comparisons without a comparison group and would be at high risk of confounding under ROBINS-E.

key_findings.finding: Sampling: about 13,760 Army enlisted men returned from Vietnam to the United States in September 1971; a random 'general sample' of 470 was drawn from them, and a random 'drug-positive sample' of 495 from the about 1,400 whose departure urine was positive for narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates; 22 men were in both samples, 943 in all. Between May and September 1972, 8 to 12 months after return, 95% were interviewed, 92% gave urine and military records were found for 99%.

Before service (general sample at arrival in Vietnam): 47% had tried an illicit drug, 41% a cannabis derivative (cannabis only, 17%), 11% a narcotic, mostly oral codeine or codeine cough syrup, and 2% heroin; under 1% had used any narcotic more than 25 times, and 13% had used any illicit drug more than a few times, almost always marijuana. Addiction to narcotics before Vietnam: 0.2% by self-report and 0.4% by the study's criteria (Table 1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pre-Vietnam Profile, tabulation (pp. 956–957) and 2nd paragraph (p. 957); Table 1 (p. 959)

key_findings.finding: In Vietnam (interviewed general sample, N=451): alcohol 92%, marijuana 69% (estimated), any of narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates 46%, narcotics 43%, amphetamines 25%, barbiturates 23%; about one third tried heroin and about one third opium, and most who tried either tried both. Of the 196 men who tried narcotics, 24% used them fewer than 5 times, 9% five or more times but not more than weekly, and more than weekly 20% for under 6 months, 23% for 6–8 months and 25% for 9 months or more; 46% reported addiction and 47% met the study's criteria, which the authors translate into 20% of the whole general sample using more than weekly for at least six months, 20% reporting addiction and 21% meeting the criteria.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use in Vietnam, 1st to 3rd paragraphs and both tabulations
key_findings.note: The in-text tabulation gives 46% for any of the three drug classes and 16% for narcotics only, while Table 1 (p. 959), for the same 451 men, gives 45% and 15% (see reporting issues). Editors' arithmetic: 48% of the 196 used more than weekly for 6 months or more (23% + 25%).

key_findings.finding: The study's addiction criteria: three of four of more-than-weekly use for more than one month; at least two withdrawal symptoms among chills, stomach cramps, insomnia and muscle pain; withdrawal lasting at least two days unmodified or 12 hours modified; and the man's belief that he was addicted.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use in Vietnam, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Narcotic use in Vietnam began early in the tour: one fifth of the men who used them started in the first week and three fifths within two months; only one fourth waited more than four months. The authors report no correlation between drug use and assignments, danger or death of friends (no statistics shown). Narcotics were mostly smoked; 40% of men using for nine months or more had injected.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use in Vietnam, 3rd paragraph (p. 957, continuing p. 958) and 5th paragraph (p. 958)

key_findings.finding: Pre-service predictors of narcotic use in Vietnam (both samples, weighted; AID and MCA, no coefficients printed): pre-service drug use, especially of several drugs, heavy drinking, arrests, not completing high school, growing up in a large city and being under 20 at arrival; first-term volunteers used drugs almost twice as often as draftees, also after controlling for the other predictors; being 24 or older best predicted avoiding drugs. No demographic characteristic predicted trying narcotics without heavy use; at least half of every group that tried narcotics used them heavily.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use in Vietnam, 7th and 8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: After return (Table 1, general sample, N=451, before / in / since Vietnam): narcotics 11% / 43% / 10%; addiction by self-report 0.2% / 20% / 0.7%; addiction by the study's criteria 0.4% / 21% / 1%; amphetamines 24% / 25% / 19%; barbiturates 14% / 23% / 12%; marijuana 41% / 69% / 45%. About half of the men who used narcotics in Vietnam had become addicted, against 7% of those who used them after return; only 7% thought heroin use acceptable in Vietnam and 3% in the United States.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use After Vietnam, 1st paragraph (p. 958); Table 1 (p. 959)

key_findings.finding: Remission: the authors state an addiction remission rate of 95% for men who had been addicted in Vietnam and set it beside young patients treated at the Lexington and Fort Worth federal hospitals and re-examined six months later. In the Figure, narcotic use 8 to 10 months after return among men first addicted in Vietnam was, read approximately from the plotted points: general sample (N=90) about 65% no use, 21% light use, 12% heavy use, 2% addiction; drug-positive sample (N=341) about 61%, 22%, 10% and 7%; 122 NARA patients six months after release to aftercare (ref. 5) about 11%, 6%, 14% and 70%.
key_findings.locator: Figure (p. 956); Results › Drug Use After Vietnam, 1st paragraph (p. 958)
key_findings.note: Figure values read from a 300-dpi rendering against 10-point gridlines; approximate to about 1 to 2 percentage points. Light and heavy use are not defined in this paper. An inset shows men with narcotic experience before Vietnam (N=106): about 44% no use, 33% light, 9% heavy and 12% addiction; which sample the inset uses is not stated. The 95% is not tied to either sample (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Table 2 (by use and addiction at departure; both samples combined, unweighted): still addicted, used at departure because they could not stop (n=134): 50% used any narcotic after return, 14% dependent; previously addicted and still using at departure (155): 35% and 5%; previously addicted, no use in the last 3 days (137): 33% and 5%; not addicted, still using (46): 17% and 0; not addicted, no use in the last 3 days (157): 10% and 2%; no narcotic use in Vietnam (269): 0.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use After Vietnam, 2nd paragraph (p. 958); Table 2 (p. 959)
key_findings.note: The row Ns sum to 898, all men interviewed in both samples, so the percentages mix the general and drug-positive samples without weighting (editors' arithmetic). Across the three previously addicted rows (426 men), about 8% were dependent and about 39% used any narcotic after return (editors' calculation, weighted by row N).

key_findings.finding: Timing and supply after return: men had been home on average ten months at interview; resumption of narcotics generally began within four months of return (median between the second and third month); 84% of men who used narcotics after return found a source within eight weeks, and men in all parts of the country reported ready availability; the deterrents cited most were expense, fear of addiction and fear of arrest.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use After Vietnam, 2nd paragraph (p. 958, continuing p. 959)

key_findings.finding: Heavy use did not fall back to pre-service levels: since return, 3% had had a period of more-than-weekly narcotic use, 6% regular amphetamine use, 3% regular barbiturate use and 25% heavy marijuana use, against under 0.5%, 3%, 2% and 12% before Vietnam. After return, injection became the preferred route of 63% of men using narcotics frequently, and heroin replaced codeine as the narcotic most used; the drug-positive sample showed the same trends.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use After Vietnam, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Predictors of narcotic use after return (both samples combined): injecting narcotics in Vietnam raised the chance of later use from 9% overall to 32%, and injecting before service from 9% to 24%; weaker predictors were dependence in Vietnam or earlier in service, heavy barbiturate or amphetamine use in Vietnam, more than six months of narcotic use in Vietnam and low rank; pre-service predictors were weaker than in-service ones.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use After Vietnam, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Table 3 (general-sample men who used narcotics in Vietnam, N=196, by drug used after return: narcotic n=43 / amphetamine or barbiturate n=49 / marijuana only n=71 / none n=33): perceived drug-related problem 23% / 7% / 11% / 6%; non-traffic arrest 49 / 22 / 25 / 15; psychiatric treatment 26 / 12 / 6 / 12; depressive syndrome 16 / 14 / 10 / 3; unemployed (out of service 6 months or more) 38 / 14 / 19 / 10; divorced (ever married) 42 / 36 / 28 / 7; alcoholism 12 / 6 / 13 / 6. Symbols mark the narcotic group as significantly higher for drug-related problem, arrest, psychiatric treatment and unemployment, and men using any drug as higher than men using none for divorce.

Among men who used no narcotics after return, those who had used narcotics in Vietnam had more arrests than those who had not, but no other statistically significant ill effects, holding other drug use since return constant (no data shown). In the multivariate analysis, drug use in and before Vietnam was the strongest predictor of post-return arrests, depression, unemployment and divorce (no coefficients shown).
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use and Post-Vietnam Adjustment, 3rd paragraph (p. 959, continuing p. 960) and 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Validity checks: 97% of men whose military records showed heroin use in Vietnam admitted it at interview; only 16% of men whose interview urine was positive had expected a positive result, and only 42% of those expecting one had it; 97% of men interviewed gave a urine specimen large enough to test. The proportion of positive specimens is not given.

The authors contrast their remission with earlier US follow-ups of hospitalized patients (relapse 80% to more than 90%, readdiction over 70%; refs 5–8), conclude that in certain circumstances people can use narcotics regularly and even become addicted yet stop in another social setting, and leave open whether the men's backgrounds or the change of setting explains the remission. They list as limits the atypical setting, a sample homogeneous in age, sex, occupation and period, the short tour, possible concealment and unknown generalizability, and plan a three-year follow-up with a matched nonveteran group.

Pre-service characteristics associated with pre-service drug use (arrests, unemployment, race, early drunkenness, truancy, large city, age, parental problems) together explained only 10% of its variance.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes the drug-positive sample as men whose urine was positive for opiates at departure (p. 955); the Methods say it was drawn from men whose urine was positive for illicit drugs, defined as narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates (p. 956).
reporting_issues.consequence: The drug-positive sample may include men detected for amphetamines or barbiturates only; results for that sample (Figure, Table 2) should not be described as results for men who tested positive for opiates.

reporting_issues.issue: The 95% remission rate for men addicted in Vietnam is given without its sample or denominator (p. 958). The Figure shows about 2% (general sample) and about 7% (drug-positive sample) addicted again, and the three previously addicted rows of Table 2 give about 8% dependent after return (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 95% cannot be reproduced from the printed data; claims should give the sample-specific figures and say that 'remission' meant not being addicted again within 8 to 12 months, with many men still using narcotics.

reporting_issues.issue: Neither Table 2 nor its footnote says that it combines the general and drug-positive samples, and no weighting is mentioned; by the editors' arithmetic its row Ns (134, 155, 137, 46, 157, 269) sum to 898, the number interviewed in both samples (title, p. 955).
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 2 percentages over-represent men detected at departure; they describe groups defined by departure status, not the population of returnees.

reporting_issues.issue: For the same interviewed general sample (N=451), the in-text tabulation of drug use in Vietnam gives 46% for any of narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates and 16% for narcotics only (p. 957), while Table 1 gives 45% and 15% (p. 959).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; one-point differences that do not change any conclusion, but a claim should cite one source and say which.

reporting_issues.issue: The Figure is captioned as narcotic use eight to ten months after Vietnam (p. 956), while interviews took place 8 to 12 months after return (p. 956, Methods) and averaged about ten months (p. 958).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the window behind the Figure is not stated precisely.

reporting_issues.issue: The pre-service profile tabulation is introduced as describing the general sample of 470 (p. 956), but only status, age and education came from military records; the drug-experience rows can only come from the 451 interviews.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the denominator for pre-service drug experience is probably 451, as in Table 1.

reporting_issues.issue: Significance in Table 3 is shown only by symbols, with no test, statistic or p value; the text says men who kept using narcotics after return exceeded the other men who had used narcotics in Vietnam in depression and divorce (p. 960), but Table 3 marks neither of these comparisons as significant, and the significant unemployment difference is not mentioned in that sentence.
reporting_issues.consequence: The depression and divorce differences between post-return narcotic use and other drug use should not be cited as statistically supported.

reporting_issues.issue: The Comment says the cohort was not preselected on any variable known to predispose to drug use (p. 961), which is true of the general sample but not of the drug-positive sample, selected on a positive urine test and used in the predictor analyses.
reporting_issues.consequence: Generalizability arguments for the predictor analyses rest on the weighting of the drug-positive sample, which is described only briefly (p. 958).

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record, journal download), pp. 955–961 (all 7 pages; old scan with an incomplete text layer, so every number was checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi, and Tables 1–3 and the Figure were re-rendered and read at 300 dpi; Figure values read approximately from the plotted points; no supplement; the 1974 monograph (ref. 1) with the full data was not read).
